title: Out There
description: * Reminder: The Savor of the Month theme for October is WATER. Details here ; Supporters can share their findings in the thread here . Check it out! “Writing in the places that shape and sustain us.” Fall (or at least post-summer) finally seems to be arriving here in New Orleans. And it is almost time — wherever you are — for Write Out . This is an annual undertaking of the National Writing Project , developed in conjunction with the National Park Service . As I wrote last year : The core idea is pretty simple: get outside, and write. Write about your environment, write to your environment, observe and attend to nature, use the craft of writing to sharpen your senses, and use your senses to sharpen your writing. “The goal is to be inspired by the world around us ,” the NWP writes, “and to connect and learn through place-based writing and sharing.” Nothing (well, maybe apart from the actual weather) is stopping you from writing outside any time. But Write Out is a kick in the pants, a kind of open-to-anyone annual two-week event, which the NWP promotes through various prompts and other resources aimed at educators but available to all. This year Write Out happens October 11–25, with the lovely theme Write Where We Stand — “writing in the places that shape and sustain us.” Every year NWP publishes a “ choice board ” of theme-related prompts; here are a few (condensed and slightly modified versions) of my favorites for this year. (Click through on each prompt title for the full NWP context/instructions.) Poetically Advocate A Place You Love . Take inspiration from Don Welch’s poem “ Advice From a Provincial ,“ and identify three “outdoor images or phenomena that are wondrous about your place. Use them to create a poetic letter to someone who doesn’t really know” the place you love, or at least not like you know it. Link Words and Image s. Snap some pictures around your community. Take your time. Choose one that captures something to celebrate — and one that captures something you would like to change. Pair these images. “ What story do they tell when you look at them together? Give your story a title, caption your images, and share your work.” Speak Like A River. Poets Amanda Eke and Mario José Pagán Morales consider the Bronx River, and what stories it might tell. In a place you know, reflect on “ what that place has witnessed , remembered, celebrated, protected, or survived. … If this river, tree, park, or wooded pathway could talk — tell us poems, tell us stories — what do you think it would say?” Write about it. Leave a comment THERE’S MORE! In connection with Write Out, there are two online events that sound cool: Hawaiian Kilo: Writing Rooted in Place Native Hawaiians developed a practice known as Kilo — “to watch, observe, examine, or forecast.” This means closely observing the natural world and its patterns, ideally to better steward the environment. A Zoom workshop, “led by teachers from the Waiākea Intermediate School in Hilo Hawai'i,” happens October 13, 2026, 6 pm US Central time . Details and (free) registration here . Haiku + Comic = Haikomic The Write Time with Write Out Ambassador Grant Snider on October 20 . Snider is a writer/artist who combines haiku with comics. (Details on that here , and at his newsletter. ) And he is this year’s Write Out Author Ambassador. Check the Write Out newsletter for event details as they emerge. I really like the sound of this and hope to revisit. Grant Snider, via Incidental Comics Leave a comment PS I was a Write Out Ambassador last year. I love Write Out! title: Step by step: How to find Design System + AI jobs faster with Claude Code and MCP
description: I gave our Design System job board an MCP server. Your AI agent can read the whole job board now. (What is an MCP? MCP is the standard that lets an agent call a tool instead of scraping a web page) Into Design Systems + AI is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. Why? Good roles go early. By the time you have scrolled the job board and opened twelve tabs and read the postings properly the pile on the recruiter’s desk is deep. There are 225 open Design System roles on the board right now. Every one of them is checked by hand and closed postings drop out. Nobody reads 225 postings. You read four and apply to two. Your agent works through all of them. It runs at https://jobs.intodesignsystems.com/mcp It needs no key and no account and it can only read Below are the 30 prompts I run against it The last ones hand the whole job over to a cron job that checks the board every morning for you What is inside One line to connect the server. Everything after it is a prompt. 23 prompts for finding roles and reading salary bands and closing skill gaps and preparing for the interview. 7 prompts that hand the search to a cron job so your Mac checks the board while you sleep. The five tools and what each one answers. Step 1: connect it One line in your terminal (1 min) Paste this in Claude Code: claude mcp add -s user --transport http ids-jobs https://jobs.intodesignsystems.com/mcp The -s user part registers it for every folder. Leave it out and the server only exists in the folder you happened to be in. Then restart Claude Code once because tools load when a session starts. Quit it with /exit and start it again and ask “which tools do you have from ids-jobs?” No terminal at all? Claude Desktop and claude.ai do it in the interface: Settings then Connectors then Add custom connector. Paste the URL and start a new chat. Cursor and every other MCP client work too. The setup page has the config for each of them. Step 2: the prompts Put your CV in the folder you start Claude Code in or simply describe your skills. Then use these. Every number under a prompt is what the board answered on 21 August 2026. I want the roles that are worth my time Five prompts that cut 225 postings down to the handful you would actually take. 1. “Which Design System roles were posted in the last two weeks? Optional: Which of them fit my CV?” The one I use most. 57 roles came in over the last fourteen days. Here are the five newest: Malt Head of Experience Systems & AI France / Germany 21 Aug ICEYE Staff/Lead Product Designer, Design System Finland 21 Aug eBay Principal Designer - Design Systems USA 21 Aug Figma Product Designer, AI Models USA remote 21 Aug Harvey Product Designer, Design Systems USA 21 Aug Your agent then keeps the ones that match your CV and tells you what you are missing per role. It reads the requirements the company wrote and not the job title. 2. “Only the remote ones that ask for AI skills please” Across the whole board 32 roles are remote and name AI or agentic skills in the posting. Those are the ones I would read first. 3. “Compare the Netflix and the General Motors role for me. Which one is closer to what I have done?” Two postings side by side with your CV as the yardstick. 4. “Put the eight best matches in a table with company and title and link and one line on why it fits. Save it as shortlist.md” Now you have one working file instead of twelve open tabs. Tell it to strike the row once you have applied. 5. “Go through shortlist.md and tell me which of these roles are still open” Closed postings drop off the board so this is a real check and not a guess. Run it before you spend an evening on an application for a role that filled two weeks ago. I want a number for the salary talk Three prompts so you name a figure that came from postings and not from a feeling. 6. “What do postings pay for a Staff level Design System role?” 46 postings state a range themselves. The median sits between 162,600 and 220,000 USD and the highest range on the board tops out at 710,000. Almost all of those postings are US roles because pay transparency laws require the number there so do not carry them into another country. 7. “Which US roles ask for design tokens and what do they pay?” 17 US postings name design tokens. Eleven of them state a range and four of those top out above 200,000 USD. The highest is the Netflix Systems Designer role in Design Foundations at 260,000 to 400,000. 8. “This posting states no salary. What do comparable roles on the board pay?” You get the range from the postings that do state one plus which level and country they came from. That is a reference point and not their budget. Say the number first anyway. I want to know what to learn next Four prompts for the months when you are not applying and want to be ready when you are. 9. “Which skills come up in most postings that my CV does not mention?” Run this when you are not applying yet. It tells you what to learn next instead of guessing. 93 of the 135 postings we hold the full text for ask for AI or agentic skills. 10. “Read the Netflix posting. Which requirements do I not have yet and where do I learn them?” The server does not stop at the gap. find_learning takes the missing skill and helps you find where to learn it. It names the recorded conference session from the Into Design Systems AI Conference that covers it. Ask about MCP and you get Diana Wolosin , Netflix (ex Indeed) on machine-readable design systems for MCP and LLMs. Ask about agentic design systems and you get Romina Kavcic on the five agentic flows. 11. “Which roles do not ask for AI skills at all?” 48 of the described postings ask for none. Useful if you are still building that muscle and want something you can start on Monday. 12. “Which words do these postings use for the work I already do?” Vocabulary research and nothing else. You still write your own CV but you write it in the words the market uses. I want to walk into the interview prepared Four prompts that turn their own posting into your prep sheet. 13. “Read this posting and tell me the three things they care about most and what I should have ready as evidence” My prep prompt. You get their own wording back plus the questions worth preparing for. 14. “What does this posting not ask for?” Stops you preparing three days for a topic nobody will bring up. 15. “Give me three questions to ask them at the end. Base them on their own posting” Questions that come out of their requirements land differently than the ones everybody asks. 16. “Which companies have more than three roles open?” General Motors has 5 and Netflix has 4. Coinbase and ESET and Yassir have 3 each. Several roles open at once usually means a team is being built. Worth a direct message. I want to know where the roles are Four prompts before you plan a move or a timezone or a year of applications. 17. “Where do most Design System roles sit right now?” USA has 119 and the United Kingdom 16 and Germany 14. Canada and France have 12 each. Useful if you are weighing a move or a timezone. 18. “How many of the German roles can be done remotely?” One of the 14. Ask that before you spend a year applying from a country you do not want to move to. 19. “How concentrated is the board? How many companies are hiring and how many have more than one role?” 190 companies are hiring right now and 27 of them have two or more roles open. 20. “Are there contract roles?” Seven right now. get_job carries the employment type so you can sort permanent from contract before you read anything. I am the one hiring Three prompts for the other side of the table. 21. “Compare our job description against the open Design System postings and tell me what other companies name that we leave out” You get back what the other postings name and your description leaves out. 22. “What do other companies call this role?” 88 of the open postings carry Design System Designer in the title and 94 carry Product Designer and 23 carry Design System Engineer. 98 say Staff or Senior. Name the role the way the people you want are searching. 23. “Who are we competing with for these people right now?” Every company with an open role in your corner of the board plus how many they have open. That is your candidate’s other tab. Step 3: let it check the board every morning A cron job is your Mac running something on a schedule without you. You never have to write one. You describe what should happen and when and Claude Code sets it up. The daily check Save your CV as cv.md in a folder. Mine is ~/jobs . Start Claude Code in that folder and paste this. 24. “Set up a job check that runs every weekday at 8 in the morning. Read cv.md in this folder. Ask the ids-jobs server for the roles posted in the last seven days that can be done remotely and keep the ones that fit my CV. Write them into today.md with one line per role: company and title and why it fits. If nothing fits write nothing new. It has to run on its own without asking me anything because I am not at the machine at 8. Put it in my crontab and run it once now so I can see that it works.” Claude writes the script and sets the schedule and shows you the first result. Here is what came back for me: SAP Senior UX Designer - Design Systems Microsoft Principal Product Designer, Design Systems Netflix Systems Designer, Design Foundations Clio Staff Product Designer, Design Systems Babylist Staff Product Designer, AI Builder Two things to know before you run it. The one click you have to give: Claude asks before it edits your crontab. Say yes and it is done. Full Disk Access: on macOS your terminal needs it under System Settings then Privacy and Security. Without it the 8 o’clock run cannot read your CV. Four more worth scheduling The daily check is one job. These four run next to it. 25. “Same thing but once a week. Monday at 9. Everything from the last seven days grouped by country and put the remote ones first” The daily one is for an active search. This is the version you keep running when you are not looking. It takes two minutes to read on Monday. 26. “Watch Figma and Netflix and Atlassian for me. Check every morning and only write something into watch.md when one of them posts a new Design System role” For the three companies you would leave for. Silence most days is the point. 27. “On the first of every month ask for the hiring numbers and append them to market.md with the date. Open roles and remote share and AI share and the salary range” After four months you have your own trend line. The board only tells you today and the file tells you the direction. 28. “Send the result to name@example.com instead of writing a file” Add that sentence to any of the prompts above and it lands in your inbox. Checking and stopping it You never open crontab yourself. You ask. 29. “Show me what you scheduled and when it runs next” 30. “Stop the daily job check but leave the Monday one running” You never touch crontab yourself. You say what you want and Claude edits it. What it does not do It does not apply for you: every role links to the employer’s own page and the server never sends anything on your behalf. It should not write your cover letter: a letter that came out of a model reads like one. Use this to work out what the role wants and then write it yourself. It only knows Design System and AI design roles: nothing else is on the board. Try it claude mcp add -s user --transport http ids-jobs https://jobs.intodesignsystems.com/mcp Setup page with all clients: jobs.intodesignsystems.com/mcp-guide . The board itself lives at jobs.intodesignsystems.com . A longer version of this walkthrough lives on our blog. It adds what to put in cv.md so the matching actually works plus a troubleshooting table for the things that go wrong: read it on intodesignsystems.com . Good luck! You got this! If you get stuck or you have an idea for a tool the server should have then write me on LinkedIn . Sil Bormüller Founder @ Into Design Systems P.S. Missing the AI skills these roles ask for? Level up. The Into Design Systems AI conference has hands-on talks on AI workflows and Claude Code and Cursor and Design System automation from industry experts. title: What A Coincidence
description: * This was meant to go out yesterday, but there was a glitch on my end. Sorry! * Reminder: The Savor of the Month theme for September is STRIPES. Details here ; Supporters can share their findings in the thread here . So many great contributions! Check it out ! “ coincidence ,” by K Bahr on Flickr “A coincidence, after all, has to be noticed.“ Dear friend of TAoN Suzanne M sent me a link the other day to a deep-dive article about coincidences . I’d never given this subject much thought, but it turned out to be pretty interesting. And as Suzanne detected, there was a noticing/attention angle that I couldn’t help dwelling on. A coincidence, after all, has to be noticed. If I walk past a childhood friend I haven’t seen in 20 years in some airport where neither of us lives, one of us has to notice the other for the coincidence to “count,” as it were. In some ways, “ the amazing thing is not that these things occur, it’s that we notice them, ” according to David Spiegelhalter, a professor at the University of Cambridge who studies such things, as quoted in Julie Beck’s’ Atlantic article. You could say that being more attentive leads to registering more coincidences. Spiegelhalter, the article notes, has a website where people can submit their coincidence experiences, and claims to have collected something like 5,000 of them. The most common form is “ finding a link with someone you meet .” Obviously, this suggests that people who are looking for connections — who are open, curious, attentive to others — are more likely to find unexpected ones. “Coincidences never happen to me at all, because I never notice anything,” Spiegelhalter says (somewhat jokingly). “I never talk to anybody on trains. If I’m with a stranger, I don’t try to find a connection with them … .” I admit it never really occurred to me that there could be coincidence-friendly types . But Beck also cites another researcher who has found that certain personality traits are linked to experiencing more coincidences—people who describe themselves as religious or spiritual, people who are self-referential (or likely to relate information from the external world back to themselves), and people who are high in meaning-seeking are all coincidence-prone. The article goes on to explore everything from Jung’s idea of synchronicity to popular notions of the paranormal. Possibly the opposite of missing coincidences is reading too much meaning into mere chance occurrences that look like something more. The world shapes our attention, but sometimes attention shapes our world — for better or worse! That said, I’m attracted to this idea that “finding a link with someone you meet” is the most-reported form of coincidence. It’s a nice frame for chatting with someone new: Be curious, be open — and look for a happy coincidence or two. Leave a comment Thank you Suzanne! Noticing is about other people, too. title: Wild, As In Harmonious
description: * Reminder: The Savor of the Month theme for September is STRIPES. Details here ; Supporters can share their findings in the thread here . So many great contributions! Check it out ! “You need to go out into the world and look.” If you pay attention to the idea of paying attention, you have no doubt encountered the words of Mary Oliver, from her poems, essays, interviews. Oliver attracted fans ranging from John Waters to Oprah, from Stephen Colbert to Lucy Dacus. In The Art of Noticing book, I quoted from her poem “ Sometimes ”: Instructions for living a life: Pay attention. Be astonished. Tell about it. But the truth is, I didn’t really know much about Oliver’s life, and even my familiarity with her work was pretty thin. So I was very excited to see the new documentary about her, Mary Oliver: Saved By the Beauty of the World, via the PBS series American Masters. You can watch on the PBS site , or on YouTube . I recommend it! The documentary covers Oliver’s career as well her personal life, traumas included. (The title borrows from her line: “I got saved by poetry, and I got saved by the beauty of the world.”) I won’t attempt to summarize the whole thing, but I’ll share some of of the TAoN- relevant highlights. Oliver grew up in Ohio, an outsider drawn mostly to the natural world and “dead poets.” She preferred noticing to being noticed. Later, in her 20s, she learned from the intensity with which her partner, photographer Molly Malone Cook, interacted with others. Another of her familiar quotations: “ Attention without feeling … is only a report. ” Oliver and Cook lived in Provincetown, where Oliver continued her practice, attentive and poetic, walking the same paths to discover what she missed before. In time, she won major awards, and a significant audience, but to some extent the literary establishment pigeonholed her as someone who basically just went for walks and wrote about it. One person in the documentary calls her an icon of the hermit life. But that’s not the whole story. “You need to go out into the world and look,” the poet Mark Doty says in the documentary, and that’s exactly what Oliver was doing — even if it was in the nearby woods. Her appreciation of the natural world was no retreat. It was the opposite. “ Attention is the beginning of devotion, ” as she (famously) wrote in the title essay of her collection Upstream . This is perhaps her central lesson for those of us who care to go out into the world land look. “You can get ecstatic over a box of matches,” she remarks in one interview clip. And in other she makes the point I love the most: “If you love something, you give it a lot of attention. And if you give something a lot of attention, you very often learn to love it.” Yet another widely quoted Oliver line is her poetic question : “ what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life? ” Her own life might not sound “wild” in the way we commonly use that word. But if you don’t have time for the whole documentary, check out the clip below discussing her poem “ Wild Geese ” — and ultimately pointing out that wild can also mean natural, harmonious. description: Welcome to the latest edition of OBJECTS QUARTERLY, a roundup of object-related items of interest published, uh, quarterly, for supporters of The Art of Noticing. Attending to objects is a sub-theme of TAoN, and a favorite subject of mine. Revisit prior OQ issues, and other mindful materialism posts, here . Enjoy ! Via Wikipedia . By Arpingstone - Arpingstone, Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=38786 “KIM’S GAME” Today I have another object-centric attention game borrowed from fiction — borrowed twice over, in fact. It comes from a short story callled “ Kim’s Game, ” by Sadia Shepard, published in The New Yorker earlier this year. In the story, a character recalls a childhood game that his father evidently took from Rudyard Kipling’s Kim : “My father would arrange a handful of objects on a tray—an old coin, a ribbon, a rock, a thimble, that sort of thing—and ask me to memorize them. Then he’d cover the tray with a newspaper and ask me to describe what I remembered. Sometimes, he’d take something away to see if I noticed . In the Kipling novel, the game is part of Kim’s training to be a spy.” This turns out to have become a well-known game , played (with variations) by children, the Cub Scouts , the military, and others. It actually sounds like a fun exercise — and also potentially a great assignment, particularly for a writing class. (And for the record it does sound like decent spy training, too.) If you try it, or have played it in the past, tell me about it! And as always I welcome your object-centered attention games, from fiction or real life. title: Double Booked
description: * Reminder: The Savor of the Month theme for October is WATER. Details here ; Supporters can share their findings in the thread here . Check it out! Back in August, I tried a little experiment: publishing a question from my ongoing Icebreaker series as a stand-alone post, rather than a secondary item in the main newsletter. The hope was that this would encourage readers to actually answer in the comments. And it did! So I’m doing it again. All are welcome to chime in. Noticing is about other people, too. The Icebreaker series aims to help with that. There’s a central collection spot for all the icebreakers to date, here . Today’s icebreaker comes from me. What is the most recent, or most personally important, book that you’ve read twice (or more)? I would probably stipulate no children’s books; I think that’s a different discussion. But otherwise I’d be open to just seeing where the question leads — I think it’s somehow more interesting than just asking for someone’s “favorite” book. This subject of re-reading books has popped up randomly a couple of times for me lately, and made me think about how long it’s been since I’ve done it. I guess I now worry that I just don’t have enough time to repeat a book when there are so many I haven’t read once! That said, the most recent was The Ladies’ Paradise , by Zola, which I read for a second time about 10 years ago. The book I’ve read the most times is Native Son , three times (all in my 20s, I believe). What about you? Love to hear your thoughts! Leave a comment And please send your favorite icebreaker (whether you made it up or found it elsewhere) to consumed@robwalker.net . Previously: OKAY THAT’S IT! As always, I value your feedback (suggestions, critiques, positive reinforcement, constructive insults directed at me, not at anyone else , etc.), as well as your tips or stories or personal noticing rituals, things we need a word for, and of course your icebreakers : consumed@robwalker.net. Or use the comments. —> Or just click the heart symbol. That always makes my day. Share The Art of Noticing And thanks for reading … rw All this by Rob Walker (unless otherwise noted) PO Box 171, 748 Mehle St., Arabi LA 70032. Pics via SignedPG Hi all, I was thinking about saving this for the next Objects Quarterly , but it deserves its own post. Here’s the story. A few weeks ago I shared an icebreaker question suggested by valued reader Judi K: “What is something you decided not to spend money on — that you now wish you had?” Among the dozens of great answers was a little tale from SignedPG about his rather charming interest in the Big Boy restaurant chain, and his resulting collection of Big Boy items involving its amusing mascot/logo character . This sparked a bit of a sub-thread about Big Boy, but that’s another matter. For today’s purposes, here’s the key passage from SignedPG: During a road trip my partner and I went into this huge antique/vintage store, and right in the front was this Big Boy plastic figurine. It was $40, maybe the size of a Coke bottle, and I wanted it badly. The problem was that in the moment I convinced myself that my collection was stupid. I saw my reflection in the glass display, and I was just mean to myself. He still thinks about this decision, with regret: “I should’ve bought that stupid piece of plastic, but really, I just wish I was nicer to myself.” And then, a few weeks after sharing this story, a funny thing happened.
